overview: This broad atlas label covers changing parts of Chile and western Argentina from 1500 BCE to an indexed endpoint of 1800 CE. It does not identify one people or an unchanged way of life. The outline contracts southward and inland over time, while real communities combined hunting, gathering, farming and herding in different ways. The examples below distinguish specific archaeological sites from later Pehuenche communities; they are not a single ancestral nation.

periods.title: An imported starting point
periods.summary: Foraging communities occupied these landscapes long before 1500 BCE. This is the atlas’s starting boundary, not a dated migration or the founding of a state. Archaeological evidence records varied local histories.

periods.title: Changing food and technology
periods.summary: In southern Mendoza, pottery and access to domesticated plants became part of some foraging economies. Uspallata followed its own path toward farming; these changes did not happen everywhere at once.

periods.title: Colonial contact and named communities
periods.summary: Later Pehuenche communities adopted horses and participated in cross-Andean exchange. The indexed endpoint is not their disappearance; the imported geometry itself ends earlier than the index.

items.text: In southern Mendoza, moving camp could follow a seasonal pattern. Archaeologists describe winter use of eastern areas and summer trips into the highlands following guanacos. Mountain snow and the uneven availability of rivers and springs affected those choices. Knowing when to move was a practical achievement.

At Cueva Huenul 1 in Neuquén, later occupation layers contain layers of plant material and a small hearth-like oven feature. These belong to the site’s late component, broadly the last sixteen centuries in the study. Visitors adapted a natural shelter for repeated stays, leaving traces of how they arranged their working and living space.

Huenul’s tiny stone flakes tell a story of repair. Late occupation deposits include waste from shaping and renewing cutting edges, while relatively few finished tools were abandoned. Much of the stone was local obsidian. Researchers infer that useful tools often left with their owners: the cave floor collected the workshop scraps.

Plant gathering brought variety to Huenul’s meals. Archaeobotanical work identified local wild plants across the sequence, including Prosopis pods and cactus remains. The late-Holocene layers show a wider range of plants and especially abundant Maihueniopsis cactus material. Such remains make gathered foods visible alongside the more conspicuous animal bones.

The same plant study suggests that some late visits to Huenul took place in summer, when particular foods were available. Researchers reached this interpretation by considering the plants’ seasonal availability. It gives us a small glimpse of a food calendar, without assuming that people occupied the cave throughout the year.

sections.title: New materials, changing communities and health

items.text: Mobile people could use pottery. A study of southern Mendoza compared sherds from lowlands, foothills and high mountains, mostly within the last two millennia. Makers varied wall thickness, the gritty material mixed into clay, and surface finishing. Those choices let archaeologists examine craft and mobility together; owning a pot did not automatically make its user a settled farmer.

The highland site El Indígeno contained 126 residential structures beside a meadow at about 3,500 meters. Its pottery contributes to the Mendoza study’s evidence for repeated mountain use during the late Holocene. Ceramic patterns differed across environments, prompting researchers to examine mobility, available materials and local craft choices together.

Uspallata shows why changing food cannot simply be equated with replacement by a new people. A 2026 study of forty-six ancient genomes found continuity between local foragers and later farmers. Dietary chemistry indicated fluctuating maize consumption. Farming was adopted locally, and levels of dependence changed over time. Such evidence helps distinguish the histories of neighboring communities.

The Uspallata researchers also identified later migrants around the twelfth and thirteenth centuries CE. They suggest that some moved in family groups organized through maternal relationships. These maize-dependent migrants showed nutritional stress, and ancient pathogen DNA confirmed tuberculosis. This is evidence about a particular farming population and its hardships, not a diagnosis of all foraging communities.

sections.title: Images, memory and later Pehuenche life

items.text: Huenul’s artists worked on portable objects as well as cave walls. Late-Holocene finds include painted guanaco bones, decorated gourd shell and marked plant stems. One decorated support dates to roughly the sixth or seventh century CE. Similar zigzag designs across different materials suggest shared visual conventions, although the intended messages remain uncertain.

These images are an authentic trace of communication, but the cited study does not identify a deciphered script or provide sentences we can translate. It interprets repeated imagery and visits as helping make Huenul an enduring social place. No single written language can be assigned to the atlas’s many communities across more than three thousand years.

For the later Pehuenche, the national library describes shelters made from branches and hides near streams, and family leadership associated with an elder called a lonko. This contact-period account belongs to named communities, not every earlier camp.

Pehuenche food traditions made much of the araucaria’s edible seeds, called piñones. They could be cooked or roasted and made into bread and stews. One forest food could therefore become several different meals, a useful change of menu.

After European contact, Pehuenche communities learned to ride horses and traded across the mountains. Hides, woven ponchos and bird feathers were exchanged for goods including wheat, spurs and silver. Colonial contact reshaped livelihoods without erasing the communities involved.

ending.text: The atlas’s endpoint of 1800 does not mark a shared extinction or conquest. Pehuenche communities continued afterward, despite severe nineteenth-century land losses and military expansion. Earlier archaeological traditions likewise changed through local developments and interactions, without a single regional fall. Living Indigenous peoples have their own identities and histories beyond this umbrella label.
